meta.title: LinguLab, build yourself in another language
meta.description: LinguLab is a language lab for people who want to acquire a language through years of real effort. What you watch, read, hear and meet on screen becomes study material.

hero.lead: LinguLab is a language lab for people who want to acquire a language through years of real effort. What you watch, read, hear and meet on screen becomes study material.

diagram.aria: System diagram: series, films, podcasts, books, web pages, documents and phone screenshots enter LinguMediaLab, LinguBookLab and LinguScraper, come together in LinguSync, and reach LinguFlow, Obsidian notes and email reports.

problem.title: You don't learn a language in three weeks.
paragraphs: It doesn't end when you pass an exam or finish a course and get the certificate. It takes years of keeping at it, and some days it feels endless. That is why so many people give up halfway. What I have seen in many people around me is this: they can't set up the right system, or they set one up and can't keep it going.
The reasons differ from person to person and from one learning path to another, but one pattern stood out to me:

Most apps tie you to their content, their idea of your level and their pace: the same sentences, topics that have nothing to do with you. In the flow of daily life it starts to feel like an extra job. On top of that, it can keep you away from the culture and the real world of the language you are learning. None of this seems to help people stick with a language programme.
So is it impossible to build a learning chain that is both sustainable and whole? Or what if there were tools that made it easier and gave us more flexibility?

solution.title: Learning a language is not a straight line. It happens in cycles.
intro: Each ring is a new cycle. At the start, most of your energy goes into understanding, and production takes only a small share. But as you keep going, what you can understand and what you can produce both grow, and with each ring production takes up a little more of it.

The speed and shape of this cycle are different for everyone. Learning a new language in your own country is not the same as learning it while you live where it is spoken, and your goals and motivation shape the process too. Still, the basic logic stays the same: language acquisition doesn't move in a straight line. As the cycle grows over weeks and months, you start to understand more complex things and express yourself more easily, often without noticing.

Seeing the process as a straight race can wear you out and take away your enthusiasm. Accepting that it moves in cycles, aiming for one step further each time, and tying your goal to what you really want to do in your daily or working life makes the road far more enjoyable.

Of course, how we run the process decides whether this build-up keeps going. Willpower alone can't carry a cycle that spans years. We need realistic, sustainable tools that fit the flow of life and don't pull us away from our interests and the things we want to do.
solution.ringsAria: Four nested rings. Each ring starts at the same point. Moving outward the rings grow, understanding and production both increase, and the share of production widens.
solution.caption: A conceptual diagram, not measured data. Proportions and cycle length differ from person to person.

audience.title: The point is not to find a magic method. It is to build a system you can keep up.
paragraphs: Learning a language is more than learning grammar rules. The structure of a language is limited; you can grasp its logic within a certain time. What really takes time is seeing how those rules show up in real life and in different contexts, often in completely different forms, and absorbing that over time.

On a road this long, methods that promise miracles in a short time don't work, and everyone's pace and process are different anyway. What moves you forward is the time you give the language, noticing the expressions you come across, and keeping track of what you learn. That is exactly what often gets missed: having a system you can keep up.
LinguLab grew out of that need. Instead of big promises, it has a down-to-earth goal: a flexible toolkit that helps you build your own study rhythm without upsetting your daily routine.

journey.title: The journey of a phrase
journey.lead: You meet a phrase once. The system doesn't let it go.

steps.title: Capture
steps.text: You save the phrases and sentences you come across in digital content without breaking your flow. Videos and podcasts, WhatsApp messages, translations on your phone, an article that catches your eye online, notes you take while reading an e-book: wherever it comes from, you add it to your system in one move.

steps.title: Understand
steps.text: You don't just memorise the words and phrases you saved, you really understand them. With practical AI explanations you look at the meaning both in your own language and in the target language, and you work with each one in its sentence, with its sound and context. That is what LinguMediaLab, LinguBookLab and LinguScraper are for.

steps.title: Collect
steps.text: Everything you capture from different sources comes together in one place in LinguSync and is archived in an orderly way. Phrases you save in LinguMediaLab and LinguBookLab also stay at hand in the word cards of those apps.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Before you start a new episode of a series or podcast, you can warm up by reviewing the words you saved from earlier episodes. When you are out, or have a spare moment during the day, you practise the words and sentences you have learned with the LinguFlow phone app.

steps.title: See
steps.text: You follow your progress in concrete terms. How many new words and phrases you have met and what has stuck: you see the bigger picture on the web, on your phone and in regular reports.

material.title: Anything can be study material.
material.note: When you capture chats and screenshots, the content goes only to the AI service you choose. You decide what you capture.
paragraphs: Series, films, documentaries, podcasts, books, your work documents, your chats, an article you read online. You work with whatever interests you in your target language.

You don't have to stay with artificial material made only for language learning. When you move forward with real content from your daily life, without leaving your own world behind, the process becomes far more natural, enjoyable and motivating. Your interests are already your curriculum.

science.title: We built it by looking at the evidence.
science.intro: LinguLab is built on principles from research on language acquisition and memory. That research studies methods. The effect of LinguLab itself has not been measured yet.

items.title: Comprehensible input
items.text: The density of unknown words in a text affects how much you understand. Krashen's input hypothesis is debated, but listening and reading for meaning are still seen as the foundation. In one study, watching a single full-length TV programme was enough to lead to word learning.
items.system: Studying with subtitles, listening rounds that get harder step by step, a one-tap dictionary in books.

items.title: Output and interaction
items.text: Understanding alone is not enough. Trying to produce the language yourself and using it with others also supports development.
items.system: Recording and comparing your own voice, playing a role in dialogues.

items.title: Shadowing
items.text: Studies on repeating what you hear as you hear it are promising, but results vary by person and level. In a study with 43 students in Japan, sound perception improved at both levels, while only the lower-level group improved on high-school listening questions. In a four-week training study, groups that included speaking got faster on a working memory task.
items.system: Sentence by sentence shadowing, full clip recording.

items.title: Trying to recall
items.text: Retrieving something from memory, instead of rereading it, helps you hold on to it for longer.

items.title: Spacing practice out
items.text: Spreading the same practice over time, instead of doing it in one sitting, strengthens verbal recall.
items.system: Leitner in LinguMediaLab and LinguFlow, FSRS in LinguBookLab.

items.title: Attention to form
items.text: Exposure alone is often not enough. Paying attention to the structure of the language and getting feedback also helps.
items.system: Sentence and grammar analysis, comparing your recording with the original.

items.title: Enjoyment
items.text: In a large study of foreign language learners, enjoyment came out clearly higher than anxiety. Many participants described their best moment as the one when they realised their long effort had paid off. It was a classroom study, but we think it matters: working with content you care about, at your own pace, may be one way to reach those moments more often.
items.system: Material you choose yourself, personal progress reports.

apps.title: One system, five pieces.

items.name: LinguMediaLab
items.text: Turn video and audio into subtitled study material. Shadowing, role-play and word cards in context help you hold on to what you hear.

items.name: LinguBookLab
items.text: Turn EPUB and PDF books into an interactive reading space. An offline dictionary, AI explanations and read-aloud in one place.

items.name: LinguScraper
items.text: Turn any text you select on your computer into a note and a word with one shortcut. Screenshots from your phone are processed automatically too.

items.name: LinguSync
items.text: Bring all the words and notes from different sources together in one hub. It shows you the bigger picture and produces Obsidian notes and regular progress reports.

items.name: LinguFlow
items.text: Carry everything that builds up in LinguSync in your pocket. Spaced repetition cards, word lists and your learning history, at hand any time of day.

apps.intro: Each piece focuses on one job but never stands alone: the tools at the top capture phrases from different sources, and the hub below brings everything together and turns it into daily practice.

roadmap.title: Where we are, and where we are going

founder.title: Why I built it
paragraphs: I suddenly moved to a new country. I had no idea about Dutch. Around me, dozens of people were studying Dutch in a hurry, and everyone was taking advice from everyone else.

I started with different questions: What does it mean to learn a language? How does it happen in the brain? What affects it? How did people who learned languages very different from their own manage it? As I read and watched the people around me and myself, I developed my own methods, and I saw this: it is a road of many years at the very least, with no measurable finish line.

I didn't want to read children's books or watch cartoons. I wanted to build myself, the topics I love and the work I do inside this new language too. That way I could learn the language and the culture of the society I live in at the same time.

Instead of trying to do this quickly and stressing myself out, I decided to build my own system once I had learned the structure of the language to a certain level. My aim was to turn what I learned into reflexes over the long term. When I couldn't find an app to help me, I made it myself. I use it today, and I hope it helps others who share the same aim.
